newsitem.title: UK: "Vain" Wodehouse gave Nazis a propaganda coup.
newsitem.headline: "Vain" Wodehouse gave Nazis a propaganda coup.

text.p: P.G. Wodehouse, the comic genius behind Jeeves and Bertie Wooster, was "so eaten up with vanity" that he did not realise his wartime broadcasts were a propaganda gift to the Nazis, according to files released on Monday.

Official papers, originally intended to be kept secret for at least 75 years but released early as part of British government attempts at greater openness, show Wodehouse had rather less common sense than the gormless Wooster himself.
Despite misgivings, British officials concluded that there was not enough evidence to prosecute the author for treason over the five radio talks he delivered on German radio in 1941.
But files dating from World War Two, released by the Public Record Office, show that the British government went to extraordinary lengths to keep him out of Britain during and after the war.
Officials felt his presence in Britain would have been "embarrassing".

Wodehouse, who was interned after being arrested by the Germans at his house in the French resort of Le Touquet in 1940, was adamant that he had not agreed to make the broadcasts in exchange for his freedom.

Wodehouse's broadcasts, although no more than light-hearted accounts of his experiences in a German internment camp, brought him into huge disrepute in wartime Britain, where he was seen as aiding the enemy.
In a statement to Major E.J.P. Cussen of the British security service MI5, after the liberation of Paris in 1944, Wodehouse admitted that the broadcasts had been "a hideous mistake".

But the author of more than 90 comic novels chronicling the antics of man-about-town Wooster, his manservant Jeeves, Gussie Fink-Nottle and an array of fearsome aunts, had only come to this realisation after his wife Ethel joined him in Berlin and told him the talks were going down badly in Britain.
"I never had any intention of assisting the enemy and...I suffered a great deal of mental pain as a result of my action," Wodehouse said in his statement.
He maintained that the broadcasts had been intended as a means of thanking his American fans for all the letters they had sent him while he had been interned in Germany.
"I thought that people hearing the talks would admire me for having kept cheerful under difficult conditions," he said.
He accepted payment of 250 marks from the Germans after the five talks, "not realising the implications".

The reaction to all this from British officials showed they clearly considered the famous author to be a fool with no more political sense than the Empress of Blandings, Lord Emsworth's prize pig who plays a key role in several Wodehouse novels.
Cussens, who was sent to Paris to investigate Wodehouse, described him as "lacking in wordly wisdom".
An official in London was less charitable, saying: "He was a "silly ass' and a "selfish ass' but there seems to be no point in trying to charge such an ass with treason."
Another senior official wrote in a memorandum that Wodehouse was "so eaten up with vanity and a desire for popularity that he did not fully appreciate the significance of his actions".

An American journalist, Henry Flannery of CBS who interviewed Wodehouse in Berlin during the war, said he was "a most stupid person without any political sense", who had taken part in "one of the best Nazi publicity stunts of the war".
After the war, Wodehouse settled in America and took U.S. citizenship in 1955. He was eventually given a knighthood in 1975, six weeks before he died at the age of 93.
